reported.stress: Observed. A ramp past capacity is meant to degrade; a threshold would fail the test for working.
reported.spike: Observed. Recovery is visible in the per-quarter latency, but 'recovered' is a judgement about shape rather than a number (PERF-005).
reported.concurrency: Observed. Thirty debits serialising on one row lock are meant to queue, so a p95 measures queue length rather than health. Correctness is enforced absolutely by PERF-004.

how_these_numbers_were_chosen: The order matters and was followed: baseline from CI, then PERF requirements
in requirements/requirements-catalog.md, then these thresholds. Setting a
number before there was a requirement to justify it is how an invented SLA
100 ms against an observed CI p95 of 2-7 ms is roughly fifteen times the
headroom. That is deliberate. A threshold set near the observed figure fails
on ordinary runner variance, and a gate that cries wolf gets ignored, which
is worse than no gate. This one tolerates a slow morning on shared
infrastructure and still catches a serious regression.
They are empirically derived, not business-mandated. If one is missed, the
first question is whether the target was ever right.
what_travels_between_machines: The correctness invariants hold anywhere at any speed: a concurrent debit
answering something other than 201 or 409, a 5xx, or a balance that does not
fall by exactly the amount plus fee of every success. Those are safe to fail
a build on regardless of where it runs.
Latency is not like that, which is why it is enforced only for the two
steady shapes and only in CI, where the database is a container in the same
runner. The same plan against a database across the internet measured a p95
near 37 seconds -- a figure about network distance, not about this code.
